before.claim: For each $t$, [F1] and $\beta>0$ give $|I^\beta g(t)|\le\|g\|_\infty\Gamma(\beta)^{-1}\int_0^t(t-r)^{\beta-1}dr =\|g\|_\infty t^\beta/(\beta\Gamma(\beta))$. By [F2] this is the first bound, and it also gives $I^\beta g(0)=0$.

Suppose $0\le s\le t\le T$ and put $\delta=t-s$. Since $\beta-1<0$, the kernel $(t-r)^{\beta-1}$ is no larger than $(s-r)^{\beta-1}$ for $0\le r<s$. Thus [F1] gives $$\Gamma(\beta)|I^\beta g(t)-I^\beta g(s)|\le\|g\|_\infty\left(\int_0^s\big((s-r)^{\beta-1}-(t-r)^{\beta-1}\big)dr+\int_s^t(t-r)^{\beta-1}dr\right).$$ The first integral is $(s^\beta-t^\beta+\delta^\beta)/\beta$. If $\delta=0$ it is zero. If $\delta>0$, put $q(x)=(x+\delta)^\beta-x^\beta$. It is positive, and for $x>0$ its derivative is $\beta((x+\delta)^{\beta-1}-x^{\beta-1})<0$ by [F3]; hence $0\le t^\beta-s^\beta=q(s)\le\lim_{x\downarrow0}q(x)=\delta^\beta$. Thus the first integral lies between $0$ and $\delta^\beta/\beta$. The second integral is $\delta^\beta/\beta$. Therefore the right side is at most $2\|g\|_\infty\delta^\beta/\beta$.

Divide step 1.2 by $\Gamma(\beta)>0$ and use [F2]. This gives the stated Hölder bound when $s\le t$; interchanging $s,t$ gives it for every pair. The bound tends to zero with $|t-s|$, so $I^\beta g$ is continuous.

before.quote:
Let $T>0$ and $\beta>0$. For $g\in L^1(0,T)$, its left fractional
integral of order $\beta$ is, for almost every $t\in(0,T)$,

$$I^\beta g(t):=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\beta)}\int_0^t(t-s)^{\beta-1}g(s)\,ds.$$

The definition uses Lebesgue integration, with
[[def-indefinite-lebesgue-integral-on-a-compact-interval]] and
[[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. The kernel is integrable and
$$\int_0^t(t-s)^{\beta-1}\,ds=\frac{t^\beta}{\beta}$$
by [[lem-fractional-integral-kernel-power-integral]]. Tonelli's theorem
[[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] therefore gives
$$\int_0^T\int_0^t(t-s)^{\beta-1}|g(s)|\,ds\,dt =\int_0^T|g(s)|\int_s^T(t-s)^{\beta-1}dt\,ds \le \frac{T^\beta}{\beta}\|g\|_{L^1(0,T)}<\infty,$$
so the defining integral is finite for almost every $t$. For continuous $g$,
it is finite at every $t\in[0,T]$ and
$$|I^\beta g(t)|\le \frac{t^\beta}{\beta\Gamma(\beta)}\|g\|_\infty =\frac{t^\beta}{\Gamma(\beta+1)}\|g\|_\infty,$$
using [[thm-real-gamma-functional-equation]].

For $0<\alpha<1$ and an absolutely continuous function
$u:[0,T]\to\mathbb R$, its Caputo derivative of order $\alpha$ is the
almost-everywhere defined function

$$D_C^\alpha u:=I^{1-\alpha}u'=\frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}\int_0^t(t-s)^{-\alpha}u'(s)\,ds.$$

Here absolute continuity is as in
[[def-absolutely-continuous-function]], so $u'\in L^1(0,T)$ almost
everywhere by [[thm-absolutely-continuous-functions-have-integrable-derivatives]].
The Gamma factors are the positive real Euler Gamma function
[[def-real-gamma-function-by-the-euler-integral]].
For every $s>0$, $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$, and $\Gamma(1)=1$.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

For $\beta>0$ and $t>0$,
$$\int_0^t(t-s)^{\beta-1}\,ds=\frac{t^\beta}{\beta}.$$
When $0<\beta<1$ the integral is improper at $s=t$; for $\beta\ge1$ it
is an ordinary integral. It converges in both cases because
$B(\beta,1)$ is defined for positive arguments.

For $p,q>0$, define $B(p,q)=\int_0^1t^{p-1}(1-t)^{q-1}\,dt$.

The integral is improper at both endpoints. The exact convergence theorem [[thm-real-beta-integral-convergence]] proves that it exists precisely for the displayed positive parameters and therefore discharges the definition's existence obligation.
For $p,q>0$, $B(p,q)=\Gamma(p)\Gamma(q)/\Gamma(p+q)$.
For every $s>0$, $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$, and $\Gamma(1)=1$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For $\beta>0$ and $t>0$,
$$\int_0^t(t-s)^{\beta-1}\,ds=\frac{t^\beta}{\beta}.$$
When $0<\beta<1$ the integral is improper at $s=t$; for $\beta\ge1$ it
is an ordinary integral. It converges in both cases because
$B(\beta,1)$ is defined for positive arguments.

For $s>0$, define $\Gamma(s)=\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$.

The integral is improper at both $0$ and $+\infty$. Its convergence for every $s>0$, and its failure for $s\le0$, are proved in [[thm-real-gamma-euler-integral-convergence]], which justifies the definition on exactly the displayed domain. The integrand is positive, so $\Gamma(s)>0$ throughout $(0,\infty)$.

Let $I$ and $J$ be intervals, possibly open at finite or infinite singular ends, and let $\phi:I\to J$ be a monotone differentiable surjection. Assume $\phi'$ is locally Riemann integrable and the proper change-of-variable hypotheses hold on every compact truncation. If $f$ is locally Riemann integrable on $J$, then
$$\int_J f(x)\,dx\quad\text{and}\quad\int_I f(\phi(t))|\phi'(t)|\,dt$$
converge simultaneously and, when convergent, are equal. At several singular ends this assertion is applied separately to the corresponding ends; orientation is retained for decreasing parametrizations.

before.quote:
Input $0<\alpha<1$, a step size $h>0$, an integer $N\ge1$, $\lambda\ge0$,
an initial value $u_0$, and forcing values $F^1,\ldots,F^N$. Define
$\omega_0=1$ and, for $j\ge1$,

$$\omega_j:=\frac{j-1-\alpha}{j}\,\omega_{j-1}.$$

Put $V^0=0$. For $n=1,\ldots,N$, compute

$$V^n:=\frac{F^n-\lambda u_0-h^{-\alpha}\sum_{j=1}^n\omega_jV^{n-j}}{h^{-\alpha}+\lambda},\qquad U^n:=u_0+V^n.$$

Equivalently, the discrete Caputo derivative is

$$\bar\partial_h^\alpha V^n:=h^{-\alpha}\sum_{j=0}^n\omega_jV^{n-j},$$

and the recurrence solves $\bar\partial_h^\alpha V^n+\lambda V^n=F^n-\lambda u_0$.
Since $h^{-\alpha}+\lambda>0$,
the exact-real scalar solve is nonsingular. Invalid parameters return
`invalid-input`; a finite-precision implementation that cannot certify the
solve returns `solve-failed` without reporting a value. The direct full-history
implementation uses $N(N+1)/2$ convolution terms and stores $N+1$ values; no
FFT or truncated-memory error claim is included.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $(a_k)$ and $(b_k)$ be sequences of reals and suppose there is
$K \in \mathbb{N}$ with

$$0 \;\le\; a_k \;\le\; b_k \qquad \text{for all } k \ge K .$$

Then:

1. if $\sum b_k$ converges then $\sum a_k$ converges ([[def-series]]);
2. if $\sum a_k$ diverges then $\sum b_k$ diverges.

The same statement holds verbatim for series with a general starting index $m$,
applied to the shifted sequences of [[def-series]].

The hypothesis is on the terms from some index on, not on all of them: finitely
many terms of either sequence may violate it, or be negative, without affecting
the conclusion. What may not be dropped is nonnegativity of $(a_k)$ from that
index on.

A **complex sequence** is a function $a\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb C$. Since the
additive reduct $(\mathbb C,+,0)$ of the complex field is a commutative monoid,
the finite-list construction of [[def-monoid-finite-product]], read additively,
defines its complex partial sums by
$$ S_0=0,\qquad S_{N+1}=S_N+a_N,\qquad S_N=\sum_{n<N}^{\mathbb C}a_n. $$
The superscript is omitted when the summands already make the codomain clear.

The **complex series** $\sum a_n$ converges to $s\in\mathbb C$ when
$S_N\to s$ in the metric of
[[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]; then $s$ is its sum. This is
the same finite sum and convergence as the vector-series definition on
$\mathbb R^2$ in [[def-series-of-vectors-and-rearrangement]]. The series
**converges absolutely** when the real series $\sum |a_n|$ of [[def-series]]
converges. For a bijection $\sigma\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$, its
**rearrangement along $\sigma$** is the complex series $\sum a_{\sigma(n)}$.

Let $(c_n)$ be a complex sequence and $a\in\mathbb C$. The **complex power
series centered at $a$ with coefficients $(c_n)$** is
$$ \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n(z-a)^n, $$
with powers from [[def-complex-integer-powers]] and the preceding complex
partial sums. To define its radius without ambiguity, form the specific real
power series
$$ Q(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}|c_n|x^n $$
centered at $0$. The **radius of convergence** of the complex power series is,
by definition, the radius of this $Q$ in
[[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Thus the coefficient
sequence, real variable, and center of the comparison series are all explicit.

Let $f(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_n(z-a)^n$ have radius $R$. If $|z-a|<R$, then $f$ is complex differentiable at $z$ and
$$f'(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}n c_n(z-a)^{n-1}.$$
Consequently $f$ is holomorphic on its open disc of convergence ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]).

Let $(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a sequence of reals and let $c\in\mathbb R$. The **real power series about the centre $c$ with coefficients $(a_n)$** is the series

$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(x-c)^n$$

at a real argument $x$, where powers are those of [[def-integer-power]] and convergence is that of [[def-series]]. Its value, when the series converges, is called its **sum at $x$**. At $x=c$ the series always converges to $a_0$: the term with $n=0$ is $a_0$ because $0^0=1$, and every later term is $0$.

For $r\ge0$ let $P(r)$ mean that the series converges absolutely at every real $x$ with $|x-c|<r$. The set of such $r$ contains $0$, since the condition $|x-c|<0$ has no solutions. The **radius of convergence** is

$$R:=\sup_{\overline{\mathbb R}}\{r\in\mathbb R:r\ge0\text{ and }P(r)\}\in[0,+\infty],$$

where the supremum is taken in the extended real line of [[def-extended-reals]]. Thus $R$ may be a nonnegative real or $+\infty$, but never $-\infty$.

The **open interval determined by the radius** is

$$I_R:=\{x\in\mathbb R:|x-c|<R\}.$$

When $0<R<+\infty$ this is $(c-R,c+R)$, when $R=+\infty$ it is all of $\mathbb R$, and when $R=0$ it is empty. The centre still carries the convergent value $a_0$ in the last case. No endpoint is included in $I_R$; convergence at $c-R$ or $c+R$, when these are real, is a separate question.

Let

$$f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(x-c)^n$$

have radius $R$. For every $x$ with $|x-c|<R$, the function $f$ is differentiable at $x$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$f'(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\iota(n+1)a_{n+1}(x-c)^n.$$

The differentiated series has the same radius $R$.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

For $a,b>0$ and $r,s\in\mathbb R$,
$$a^{r+s}=a^ra^s,\qquad (ab)^r=a^rb^r,\qquad (a/b)^r=a^r/b^r,\qquad (a^r)^s=a^{rs}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

The relation of [[def-real-order]] is well defined and makes $\mathbb{R}$

before.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $T>0$ and $\beta>0$. For $g\in L^1(0,T)$, its left fractional
integral of order $\beta$ is, for almost every $t\in(0,T)$,

$$I^\beta g(t):=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\beta)}\int_0^t(t-s)^{\beta-1}g(s)\,ds.$$

The definition uses Lebesgue integration, with
[[def-indefinite-lebesgue-integral-on-a-compact-interval]] and
[[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. The kernel is integrable and
$$\int_0^t(t-s)^{\beta-1}\,ds=\frac{t^\beta}{\beta}$$
by [[lem-fractional-integral-kernel-power-integral]]. Tonelli's theorem
[[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] therefore gives
$$\int_0^T\int_0^t(t-s)^{\beta-1}|g(s)|\,ds\,dt =\int_0^T|g(s)|\int_s^T(t-s)^{\beta-1}dt\,ds \le \frac{T^\beta}{\beta}\|g\|_{L^1(0,T)}<\infty,$$
so the defining integral is finite for almost every $t$. For continuous $g$,
it is finite at every $t\in[0,T]$ and
$$|I^\beta g(t)|\le \frac{t^\beta}{\beta\Gamma(\beta)}\|g\|_\infty =\frac{t^\beta}{\Gamma(\beta+1)}\|g\|_\infty,$$
using [[thm-real-gamma-functional-equation]].

For $0<\alpha<1$ and an absolutely continuous function
$u:[0,T]\to\mathbb R$, its Caputo derivative of order $\alpha$ is the
almost-everywhere defined function

$$D_C^\alpha u:=I^{1-\alpha}u'=\frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}\int_0^t(t-s)^{-\alpha}u'(s)\,ds.$$

Here absolute continuity is as in
[[def-absolutely-continuous-function]], so $u'\in L^1(0,T)$ almost
everywhere by [[thm-absolutely-continuous-functions-have-integrable-derivatives]].
The Gamma factors are the positive real Euler Gamma function
[[def-real-gamma-function-by-the-euler-integral]].

Let $T>0$, $a,b>0$, and $g\in L^1(0,T)$. Then, almost everywhere on
$(0,T)$,

$$I^a(I^b g)=I^{a+b}g.$$

Moreover,

$$\|I^a g\|_{L^1(0,T)}\le\frac{T^a}{\Gamma(a+1)}\|g\|_{L^1(0,T)}.$$

If $g\in C([0,T])$, the semigroup identity holds at every
$t\in[0,T]$. For every $c>0$ and $t\in[0,T]$,
$$I^c\mathbf 1(t)=\frac{t^c}{\Gamma(c+1)},$$
where $\mathbf 1$ is the constant function with value $1$.

Let $T>0$, $0<\beta<1$, and $g\in C([0,T])$. Then $I^\beta g$ is continuous
on $[0,T]$, $I^\beta g(0)=0$, and

$$\|I^\beta g\|_\infty\le\frac{T^\beta}{\Gamma(\beta+1)}\|g\|_\infty,$$

$$|I^\beta g(t)-I^\beta g(s)|\le\frac{2\|g\|_\infty}{\Gamma(\beta+1)}|t-s|^\beta\qquad(s,t\in[0,T]).$$

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then $F$ is differentiable for almost every $x\in(a,b)$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)$$
at every such point.

before.claim: For fixed $n$, the function $w(s)=(t_n-s)^{-\alpha}$ is positive and increasing on $[0,t_n)$, and $b_{n,k}=\Gamma(1-\alpha)^{-1}h_k^{-1}\int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k}w(s)ds$ by [F1] and [F4]. The factor $\Gamma(1-\alpha)^{-1}$ is positive by [F7]. The average of an increasing function on an earlier interval is at most its value at the shared endpoint, which is at most its average on the next interval. Each integral is finite because $\alpha<1$. Thus the weights are positive and nondecreasing in $k$.

Put $\phi(t)=t^\alpha$. By [F5], $\phi'(s)=\alpha s^{\alpha-1}$ for $s>0$, and this derivative is decreasing because its derivative is $\alpha(\alpha-1)s^{\alpha-2}<0$ and [F8] applies. It is in $L^1(0,T)$ by [F9], with integral $T^\alpha$. Its indefinite integral is $\phi(t)-\phi(0)=t^\alpha$, so $\phi$ is absolutely continuous by [F6] and its Caputo derivative is defined. On an interval $[a,b]=[t_{k-1},t_k]$ its secant slope $\bar\phi'_k$ is the average of $\phi'$, hence $e_k(s):=\bar\phi'_k-\phi'(s)$ is increasing and $\int_a^b e_k(s)ds=0$. Since $w(s)=(t_n-s)^{-\alpha}$ is also increasing, their pairwise differences have the same sign. Expanding the double integral and using $\int_a^b e_k=0$ gives $$\int_a^b e_k(s)w(s)ds=\frac1{2(b-a)}\int_a^b\int_a^b (e_k(s)-e_k(r))(w(s)-w(r))dr\,ds\ge0.$$ These integrals are finite: $e_k,w\in L^1(a,b)$, and the only possible singular product $\phi'(s)w(s)$ occurs when $n=k=1$; there it is the integrable Beta kernel $\alpha s^{\alpha-1}(t_1-s)^{-\alpha}$ from [F3]. Expanding the absolute value of the double-integral integrand bounds it by the sum of products of the finite integrals $\int|e_k|$, $\int w$, and $\int|e_k|w$, which justifies the expansion. Summing over intervals and using [F2] yields $\delta_{\mathcal T}^\alpha\phi(t_n)\ge D_C^\alpha\phi(t_n)$. Direct substitution $s=t_n y$ and [F3]–[F4] give $$D_C^\alpha(t^\alpha)(t_n)=\frac{\alpha}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}t_n^0B(\alpha,1-\alpha)=\Gamma(1+\alpha).$$ Thus, using $\Gamma(1+\alpha)>0$ from [F7], $q^n:=t_n^\alpha/\Gamma(1+\alpha)$ satisfies $q^0=0$ and $\delta_{\mathcal T}^\alpha q^n\ge1$.

Expanding [F1] by collecting coefficients gives $$\delta_{\mathcal T}^\alpha z^n=b_{n,n}z^n+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(b_{n,k}-b_{n,k+1})z^k-b_{n,1}z^0.$$ If some $z^n<0$, let $m$ be the first such index. Then $z^k\ge0$ for $k<m$, the middle coefficients in this display are nonpositive by step 1.1, and $-b_{m,1}z^0\le0$. The terms $(b_{m,m}+\lambda)z^m$ are strictly negative because $b_{m,m}>0$ and $\lambda\ge0$. Therefore $\delta_{\mathcal T}^\alpha z^m+\lambda z^m<0$, contradicting the hypothesis. This proves comparison.

For the residual equation, set $z_\pm^n:=Rq^n\pm e^n$. Then $z_\pm^0=0$ and $$\delta_{\mathcal T}^\alpha z_\pm^n+\lambda z_\pm^n =R(\delta_{\mathcal T}^\alpha q^n+\lambda q^n)\pm r^n\ge R-|r^n|\ge0.$$ Comparison from step 2.1 gives $z_\pm^n\ge0$, hence $|e^n|\le Rq^n\le RT^\alpha/\Gamma(1+\alpha)$ for every $n$. This proves residual stability.

before.quote:
Input $0<\alpha<1$, $T>0$, an integer $N\ge1$, $\lambda\ge0$, an initial
value $U^0=u_0$, and forcing values $F^1,\ldots,F^N$. Choose either the
uniform grid $t_k=kh$ with $h=T/N$, or a strictly increasing grid
$0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N=T$. A power-graded choice is
$t_k=T(k/N)^r$ with a specified $r\ge1$. Write $h_k=t_k-t_{k-1}$ and, for
$1\le k\le n\le N$, define the exact kernel weight

$$b_{n,k}:=\frac{(t_n-t_{k-1})^{1-\alpha}-(t_n-t_k)^{1-\alpha}}{\Gamma(2-\alpha)h_k}.$$

The Cauchy-sequence reals $\mathbb{R}_C$ ([[thm-reals-ordered-field]]) are
**Archimedean** ([[def-archimedean-field]]): for every $x \in \mathbb{R}_C$
there is a natural number $n$ with $x < n \cdot 1$, where the canonical natural
$n \cdot 1$ is the class $\hat n$ of the constant rational sequence $n$.
Equivalently, the canonical naturals $(\hat n)_{n \ge 1}$ are cofinal.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $(a_k)$ and $(b_k)$ be sequences of reals and suppose there is
$K \in \mathbb{N}$ with

$$0 \;\le\; a_k \;\le\; b_k \qquad \text{for all } k \ge K .$$

Then:

1. if $\sum b_k$ converges then $\sum a_k$ converges ([[def-series]]);
2. if $\sum a_k$ diverges then $\sum b_k$ diverges.

The same statement holds verbatim for series with a general starting index $m$,
applied to the shifted sequences of [[def-series]].

The hypothesis is on the terms from some index on, not on all of them: finitely
many terms of either sequence may violate it, or be negative, without affecting
the conclusion. What may not be dropped is nonnegativity of $(a_k)$ from that
index on.

**Archimedean** ([[def-archimedean-field]]): for every $x \in \mathbb{R}_C$
there is a natural number $n$ with $x < n \cdot 1$, where the canonical natural
$n \cdot 1$ is the class $\hat n$ of the constant rational sequence $n$.
Equivalently, the canonical naturals $(\hat n)_{n \ge 1}$ are cofinal.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $(a_k)$ and $(b_k)$ be sequences of reals and suppose there is
$K \in \mathbb{N}$ with

$$0 \;\le\; a_k \;\le\; b_k \qquad \text{for all } k \ge K .$$

Then:

1. if $\sum b_k$ converges then $\sum a_k$ converges ([[def-series]]);
2. if $\sum a_k$ diverges then $\sum b_k$ diverges.

The same statement holds verbatim for series with a general starting index $m$,
applied to the shifted sequences of [[def-series]].

The hypothesis is on the terms from some index on, not on all of them: finitely
many terms of either sequence may violate it, or be negative, without affecting
the conclusion. What may not be dropped is nonnegativity of $(a_k)$ from that
index on.

before.quote:
Input $0<\alpha<1$, a step size $h>0$, an integer $N\ge1$, $\lambda\ge0$,
an initial value $u_0$, and forcing values $F^1,\ldots,F^N$. Define
$\omega_0=1$ and, for $j\ge1$,

$$\omega_j:=\frac{j-1-\alpha}{j}\,\omega_{j-1}.$$

Put $V^0=0$. For $n=1,\ldots,N$, compute

$$V^n:=\frac{F^n-\lambda u_0-h^{-\alpha}\sum_{j=1}^n\omega_jV^{n-j}}{h^{-\alpha}+\lambda},\qquad U^n:=u_0+V^n.$$

Equivalently, the discrete Caputo derivative is

$$\bar\partial_h^\alpha V^n:=h^{-\alpha}\sum_{j=0}^n\omega_jV^{n-j},$$

and the recurrence solves $\bar\partial_h^\alpha V^n+\lambda V^n=F^n-\lambda u_0$.
Since $h^{-\alpha}+\lambda>0$,
the exact-real scalar solve is nonsingular. Invalid parameters return
`invalid-input`; a finite-precision implementation that cannot certify the
solve returns `solve-failed` without reporting a value. The direct full-history
implementation uses $N(N+1)/2$ convolution terms and stores $N+1$ values; no
FFT or truncated-memory error claim is included.

For $s>0$, define $\Gamma(s)=\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$.

The integral is improper at both $0$ and $+\infty$. Its convergence for every $s>0$, and its failure for $s\le0$, are proved in [[thm-real-gamma-euler-integral-convergence]], which justifies the definition on exactly the displayed domain. The integrand is positive, so $\Gamma(s)>0$ throughout $(0,\infty)$.
For every $s>0$, $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$, and $\Gamma(1)=1$.

For $x>0$ and $0\le s\le1$, $x^{1-s}\le\Gamma(x+1)/\Gamma(x+s)\le(x+1)^{1-s}$.

For $0<s<1$ both inequalities are strict. At $s=0$ the lower inequality is equality, and at $s=1$ both are equalities.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular

$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $(a_k)$ and $(b_k)$ be sequences of reals and suppose there is
$K \in \mathbb{N}$ with

$$0 \;\le\; a_k \;\le\; b_k \qquad \text{for all } k \ge K .$$

Then:

1. if $\sum b_k$ converges then $\sum a_k$ converges ([[def-series]]);
2. if $\sum a_k$ diverges then $\sum b_k$ diverges.

applied to the shifted sequences of [[def-series]].

The hypothesis is on the terms from some index on, not on all of them: finitely
many terms of either sequence may violate it, or be negative, without affecting
the conclusion. What may not be dropped is nonnegativity of $(a_k)$ from that
index on.

Let $(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a sequence of reals and let $c\in\mathbb R$. The **real power series about the centre $c$ with coefficients $(a_n)$** is the series

$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(x-c)^n$$

at a real argument $x$, where powers are those of [[def-integer-power]] and convergence is that of [[def-series]]. Its value, when the series converges, is called its **sum at $x$**. At $x=c$ the series always converges to $a_0$: the term with $n=0$ is $a_0$ because $0^0=1$, and every later term is $0$.

For $r\ge0$ let $P(r)$ mean that the series converges absolutely at every real $x$ with $|x-c|<r$. The set of such $r$ contains $0$, since the condition $|x-c|<0$ has no solutions. The **radius of convergence** is

$$R:=\sup_{\overline{\mathbb R}}\{r\in\mathbb R:r\ge0\text{ and }P(r)\}\in[0,+\infty],$$

where the supremum is taken in the extended real line of [[def-extended-reals]]. Thus $R$ may be a nonnegative real or $+\infty$, but never $-\infty$.

The **open interval determined by the radius** is

$$I_R:=\{x\in\mathbb R:|x-c|<R\}.$$

When $0<R<+\infty$ this is $(c-R,c+R)$, when $R=+\infty$ it is all of $\mathbb R$, and when $R=0$ it is empty. The centre still carries the convergent value $a_0$ in the last case. No endpoint is included in $I_R$; convergence at $c-R$ or $c+R$, when these are real, is a separate question.

Let

$$f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(x-c)^n$$

have radius $R$. For every $x$ with $|x-c|<R$, the function $f$ is differentiable at $x$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$f'(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\iota(n+1)a_{n+1}(x-c)^n.$$

The differentiated series has the same radius $R$.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

For $a,b>0$ and $r,s\in\mathbb R$,
$$a^{r+s}=a^ra^s,\qquad (ab)^r=a^rb^r,\qquad (a/b)^r=a^r/b^r,\qquad (a^r)^s=a^{rs}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Suppose $f(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_n(x-c)^n$ and $g(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}b_n(x-c)^n$ have radii $R_f,R_g$. For $|x-c|<\min(R_f,R_g)$,

$$f(x)g(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_kb_{n-k}\right)(x-c)^n,$$

and the displayed product series converges absolutely.

Let $f(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_n(x-c)^n$ have positive or infinite radius $R$. Define $f^{(0)}:=f$ and $f^{(m+1)}:=(f^{(m)})'$. Then every derivative exists on $|x-c|<R$, and for each $m\in\mathbb N$,

$$f^{(m)}(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\iota\!\left((m+j)^{\underline m}\right)a_{m+j}(x-c)^j.$$

In particular,

$$f^{(m)}(c)=\iota(m!)a_m,\qquad a_m=\frac{f^{(m)}(c)}{\iota(m!)}.$$

Let $0<\alpha<1$ and let $(\omega_j)_{j\ge0}$ be the weights defined by
[[alg-backward-euler-convolution-quadrature]]. Then the complex power series

$$W(z):=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\omega_jz^j$$

converges absolutely for every $z$ in the open unit disc
$\mathbb D=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<1\}$, and
$$W(z)=(1-z)^\alpha_{\operatorname{Log}}\qquad(z\in\mathbb D),$$
where the right side is the principal-branch power from
[[def-complex-power-from-holomorphic-logarithm-branch]]. It is well-defined
there because $1-z$ lies in the principal-logarithm slit plane.

For $x>0$ and real $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the principal branch power $x^\alpha_{\operatorname{Log}}:=\exp(\alpha\operatorname{Log}x)$ of [[def-complex-power-from-holomorphic-logarithm-branch]] equals the published real power $x^\alpha$ of [[def-real-power]]:

$$x^\alpha_{\operatorname{Log}}=x^\alpha\qquad(x>0,\ \alpha\in\mathbb R).$$

before.claim: By [F6]–[F7], $MT^\alpha/\Gamma(\alpha+1)\to0$ as $T\downarrow0$; since $T_0>0$ and $r>0$, choose $T\in(0,T_0]$ for which the displayed bound holds.

Let $B=\{u\in C([0,T]):\|u-u_0\|_\infty\le r\}$ and define $\Phi u=u_0+I^\alpha(f(\cdot,u(\cdot)))$. For $u\in B$, $s\mapsto(s,u(s))$ and then $s\mapsto f(s,u(s))$ are continuous, with $|f(s,u(s))|\le M$; [F1]–[F2] therefore make $\Phi u$ continuous and give $\|\Phi u-u_0\|_\infty\le MT^\alpha/\Gamma(\alpha+1)\le r$. Thus $\Phi$ maps $B$ into itself.

Set $u^{(0)}(t)=u_0$ and recursively $u^{(n+1)}=\Phi u^{(n)}$; step 2.1 keeps every iterate in $B$. For $n\ge1$ put $d_n(t)=|u^{(n)}(t)-u^{(n-1)}(t)|$. The bound on $f$ and [F3] give $d_1(t)\le M I^\alpha\mathbf1(t)=M t^\alpha/\Gamma(\alpha+1)$.

For $n\ge1$, Lipschitz continuity and the positive kernel [F1] give $d_{n+1}\le L I^\alpha d_n$. Starting with step 3.1, induction and the pointwise semigroup identity [F3] yield $d_n(t)\le M L^{n-1}I^{n\alpha}\mathbf1(t)=M L^{n-1}t^{n\alpha}/\Gamma(n\alpha+1)$ for every $n\ge1$.

Put $K=1+L$; then $L^{n-1}\le K^n$ for $n\ge1$, so step 4.1 and the uniform series bound [F4] show $\sum_{n=1}^\infty\|d_n\|_\infty<\infty$. The iterates are uniformly Cauchy; completeness [F5] gives a uniform limit $u\in C([0,T])$, and since every iterate lies in $B$, the norm limit also lies in $B$.

Lipschitz continuity and [F2] give $\|\Phi u^{(n)}-\Phi u\|_\infty\le (LT^\alpha/\Gamma(\alpha+1))\|u^{(n)}-u\|_\infty\to0$. Since $u^{(n+1)}=\Phi u^{(n)}$ and $u^{(n+1)}\to u$, it follows that $u=\Phi u$, proving existence in $B$.

If $u,v\in B$ are two solutions, $y=|u-v|$ is continuous and nonnegative; their equations, Lipschitz continuity, and the positive kernel [F1] give $y(t)\le L I^\alpha y(t)$ for every $t$. Applying [F4] with $A=0$ gives $y\equiv0$, hence $u=v$.

after.claim: By [F6]–[F7], $MT^\alpha/\Gamma(\alpha+1)\to0$ as $T\downarrow0$; since $T_0>0$ and $r>0$, choose $T\in(0,T_0]$ for which the displayed bound holds.

Let $B=\{u\in C([0,T]):\|u-u_0\|_\infty\le r\}$ and define $\Phi u=u_0+I^\alpha(f(\cdot,u(\cdot)))$. For $u\in B$, $s\mapsto(s,u(s))$ and then $s\mapsto f(s,u(s))$ are continuous, with $|f(s,u(s))|\le M$; [F1]–[F2] therefore make $\Phi u$ continuous and give $\|\Phi u-u_0\|_\infty\le MT^\alpha/\Gamma(\alpha+1)\le r$. Thus $\Phi$ maps $B$ into itself.

Set $u^{(0)}(t)=u_0$ and recursively $u^{(n+1)}=\Phi u^{(n)}$; step 2.1 keeps every iterate in $B$. For $n\ge1$ put $d_n(t)=|u^{(n)}(t)-u^{(n-1)}(t)|$. The bound on $f$ and [F3] give $d_1(t)\le M I^\alpha\mathbf1(t)=M t^\alpha/\Gamma(\alpha+1)$.

For $n\ge1$, Lipschitz continuity and the positive kernel [F1] give $d_{n+1}\le L I^\alpha d_n$. Starting with step 3.1, induction and the pointwise semigroup identity [F3] yield $d_n(t)\le M L^{n-1}I^{n\alpha}\mathbf1(t)=M L^{n-1}t^{n\alpha}/\Gamma(n\alpha+1)$ for every $n\ge1$, with the coefficient $L^0$ at $n=1$ defined to be $1$.

Put $K=1+L$; then $L^{n-1}\le K^n$ for $n\ge1$, so step 4.1 and the uniform series bound [F4] show $\sum_{n=1}^\infty\|d_n\|_\infty<\infty$. The iterates are uniformly Cauchy; completeness [F5] gives a uniform limit $u\in C([0,T])$, and since every iterate lies in $B$, the norm limit also lies in $B$.

Lipschitz continuity and [F2] give $\|\Phi u^{(n)}-\Phi u\|_\infty\le (LT^\alpha/\Gamma(\alpha+1))\|u^{(n)}-u\|_\infty\to0$. Since $u^{(n+1)}=\Phi u^{(n)}$ and $u^{(n+1)}\to u$, it follows that $u=\Phi u$, proving existence in $B$.

Let $T>0$ and $\beta>0$. For $g\in L^1(0,T)$, its left fractional
integral of order $\beta$ is, for almost every $t\in(0,T)$,

$$I^\beta g(t):=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\beta)}\int_0^t(t-s)^{\beta-1}g(s)\,ds.$$

The definition uses Lebesgue integration, with
[[def-indefinite-lebesgue-integral-on-a-compact-interval]] and
[[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. The kernel is integrable and
$$\int_0^t(t-s)^{\beta-1}\,ds=\frac{t^\beta}{\beta}$$
by [[lem-fractional-integral-kernel-power-integral]]. Tonelli's theorem
[[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] therefore gives
$$\int_0^T\int_0^t(t-s)^{\beta-1}|g(s)|\,ds\,dt =\int_0^T|g(s)|\int_s^T(t-s)^{\beta-1}dt\,ds \le \frac{T^\beta}{\beta}\|g\|_{L^1(0,T)}<\infty,$$
so the defining integral is finite for almost every $t$. For continuous $g$,
it is finite at every $t\in[0,T]$ and
$$|I^\beta g(t)|\le \frac{t^\beta}{\beta\Gamma(\beta)}\|g\|_\infty =\frac{t^\beta}{\Gamma(\beta+1)}\|g\|_\infty,$$
using [[thm-real-gamma-functional-equation]].

For $0<\alpha<1$ and an absolutely continuous function
$u:[0,T]\to\mathbb R$, its Caputo derivative of order $\alpha$ is the
almost-everywhere defined function

$$D_C^\alpha u:=I^{1-\alpha}u'=\frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}\int_0^t(t-s)^{-\alpha}u'(s)\,ds.$$

Here absolute continuity is as in
[[def-absolutely-continuous-function]], so $u'\in L^1(0,T)$ almost
everywhere by [[thm-absolutely-continuous-functions-have-integrable-derivatives]].
The Gamma factors are the positive real Euler Gamma function
[[def-real-gamma-function-by-the-euler-integral]].

Let $T>0$, $0<\beta<1$, and $g\in C([0,T])$. Then $I^\beta g$ is continuous
on $[0,T]$, $I^\beta g(0)=0$, and

$$\|I^\beta g\|_\infty\le\frac{T^\beta}{\Gamma(\beta+1)}\|g\|_\infty,$$

$$|I^\beta g(t)-I^\beta g(s)|\le\frac{2\|g\|_\infty}{\Gamma(\beta+1)}|t-s|^\beta\qquad(s,t\in[0,T]).$$

Let $T>0$, $a,b>0$, and $g\in L^1(0,T)$. Then, almost everywhere on
$(0,T)$,

$$I^a(I^b g)=I^{a+b}g.$$

Moreover,

$$\|I^a g\|_{L^1(0,T)}\le\frac{T^a}{\Gamma(a+1)}\|g\|_{L^1(0,T)}.$$

If $g\in C([0,T])$, the semigroup identity holds at every
$t\in[0,T]$. For every $c>0$ and $t\in[0,T]$,
$$I^c\mathbf 1(t)=\frac{t^c}{\Gamma(c+1)},$$
where $\mathbf 1$ is the constant function with value $1$.

Let $T>0$, $0<\alpha<1$, $A,L\ge0$, and let $y\in C([0,T])$ be
nonnegative. If
$$y(t)\le A+L I^\alpha y(t)\qquad(0\le t\le T),$$
then for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$y(t)\le A\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{L^k t^{k\alpha}}{\Gamma(k\alpha+1)}.$$
The $k=0$ term is $1$, including when $L=0$, and the series converges
uniformly on $[0,T]$. In particular, if $A=0$ then $y\equiv0$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$. Then the closed bounded interval
$[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]]) is compact ([[def-open-cover-r]]): every family of
open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ whose union contains $[a,b]$ has a finite subfamily
whose union already contains $[a,b]$.

The proof is by repeated bisection. Supposing some open cover admits no finite
subcover, one halves the interval, keeps a half that still admits none, and
iterates; the halves shrink to a point, which the cover does reach, and a single
member of the cover then swallows a whole late-stage half. **The halving rule is
canonical**, taking the left half whenever the left half works, so the recursion
uses [[thm-recursion]] and no choice principle.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open sets as in
[[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]].

- An **open cover** of $(X,d)$ is a family $\mathcal{U}$ of open subsets of $X$
  with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$, where
  $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily
  $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$ that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \emptyset$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,d)$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite subcover: for
  every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \emptyset$ and the empty subfamily
  covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the metric
  subspace $(A, d_A)$ is a compact metric space, $d_A$ being the restriction of
  $d$ to $A \times A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A,d_A)$ and its own open sets, not
about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do agree,
but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]], and no item of this library may use the
ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading as the
definition is what makes "compact" a property of the metric space $(A,d_A)$
alone, so that a set compact in one ambient space is compact in every other one
containing it isometrically.

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. The
one-point space is compact too, and so is every space listed as
$\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$: given a cover, each $x_i$ lies in some member, and
finitely many members chosen in this way already cover.

**The finiteness convention, and how it is used both ways.** "Finite" above is
the listing form, matching the finite lists of
[[def-finite-intersection-property]]. It agrees with the definition of
finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number ([[def-countable]]), and
both directions of the agreement are available and are used below:

- A nonempty finite set $F$ in the sense of [[def-countable]] satisfies
  $F \approx m$ for some $m \ge 1$, and a bijection $m \to F$ is exactly a
  listing $F = \{a_0, \dots, a_{m-1}\}$.
- Conversely a set listed as $A = \{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$, that is the image of a
  function $a$ with domain $\sigma(n)$, is finite in the sense of
  [[def-countable]]: the map sending $x \in A$ to the least $i \le n$ with
  $a_i = x$ is an injection of $A$ into $\sigma(n)$, so $A$ is equinumerous with
  a subset of $\mathbb{N}$ bounded above, and such a subset is finite
  ([[lem-subset-of-countable]]).

Neither direction uses a choice principle: the second selects nothing, taking a
least index instead.

Let $(K,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space. Every member of
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is bounded, so the supremum metric

$$d_\infty(f,g):=\sup_{x\in K}|f(x)-g(x)|$$

is defined on $C(K,\mathbb{R})$. With this metric,
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is complete.

Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] for $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]] for $\mathbb C$, with
induced metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ (in the complex case supplied by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]]). Then $V$ is a **Banach space** when this
metric space is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Equivalently: every Cauchy sequence in $V$ for the norm metric converges to a
point of $V$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

$(X,d)$ is **complete** if every Cauchy sequence in $(X,d)$
([[def-cauchy-in-metric]]) converges to a point of $X$
([[def-metric-convergence]]).

A subset $A \subseteq X$ is called **complete** when the metric subspace
$(A, d_A)$ is complete ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]); as always, the
metric is part of the data, and $d_A$ is the restriction of $d$ to $A \times A$.

**The limit is unique when it exists**, since limits in a metric space are unique
([[lem-metric-limits-unique]]), so a complete space assigns to each of its Cauchy
sequences one point and not a set of points.

**Completeness is a property of the pair $(X,d)$, not of $X$ and not of the
topology of $d$.** Both quantifiers in the definition are about the metric: the
Cauchy condition is stated with distances, and so is convergence. Two metrics on
the same set can have the same open sets while exactly one of them is complete,
which is the content of [[fs-completeness-is-a-topological-property]] and its
witness. Read the word *complete* as an abbreviation for *complete with respect

For $s>0$, define $\Gamma(s)=\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$.

The integral is improper at both $0$ and $+\infty$. Its convergence for every $s>0$, and its failure for $s\le0$, are proved in [[thm-real-gamma-euler-integral-convergence]], which justifies the definition on exactly the displayed domain. The integrand is positive, so $\Gamma(s)>0$ throughout $(0,\infty)$.

$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Input $0<\alpha<1$, $T>0$, an integer $N\ge1$, $\lambda\ge0$, an initial
value $U^0=u_0$, and forcing values $F^1,\ldots,F^N$. Choose either the
uniform grid $t_k=kh$ with $h=T/N$, or a strictly increasing grid
$0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N=T$. A power-graded choice is
$t_k=T(k/N)^r$ with a specified $r\ge1$. Write $h_k=t_k-t_{k-1}$ and, for
$1\le k\le n\le N$, define the exact kernel weight

$$b_{n,k}:=\frac{(t_n-t_{k-1})^{1-\alpha}-(t_n-t_k)^{1-\alpha}}{\Gamma(2-\alpha)h_k}.$$

For a grid sequence $V^0,\ldots,V^N$, the L1 approximation to the Caputo
derivative at $t_n$ is

$$\delta_{\mathcal T}^\alpha V^n:=\sum_{k=1}^n b_{n,k}(V^k-V^{k-1}).$$

For each $n=1,\ldots,N$, return the value given by the scalar recurrence

$$U^n:=\frac{F^n+b_{n,1}U^0+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(b_{n,k+1}-b_{n,k})U^k}{b_{n,n}+\lambda}.$$

This solves $\delta_{\mathcal T}^\alpha U^n+\lambda U^n=F^n$. Every weight
$b_{n,k}$ is positive and $b_{n,n}=h_n^{-\alpha}/\Gamma(2-\alpha)>0$, so
the exact-real denominator is strictly positive. On a uniform grid, writing
$a_j=(j+1)^{1-\alpha}-j^{1-\alpha}$ gives

$$\delta_h^\alpha U^n=\frac{h^{-\alpha}}{\Gamma(2-\alpha)}\sum_{k=1}^n a_{n-k}(U^k-U^{k-1}).$$

The direct method uses every earlier increment at each step, hence uses
$N(N+1)/2$ history terms and stores $N+1$ solution values. An input outside
the stated parameter or grid domain returns `invalid-input`. A real-arithmetic
execution has no singular branch under these hypotheses; a finite-precision
implementation that cannot certify a scalar solve returns `solve-failed`
without reporting a value. The graded-grid procedure is an implementation
definition only; no optimal graded-mesh rate is part of this item.

Let $0<\alpha<1$, $\lambda\ge0$, and let
$0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N=T$ be any finite grid with $T>0$. Use the weights
$b_{n,k}$ and operator $\delta_{\mathcal T}^\alpha$ from
[[alg-uniform-and-graded-grid-l1]]. Then:

$$I^\beta g(t):=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\beta)}\int_0^t(t-s)^{\beta-1}g(s)\,ds.$$

[[def-indefinite-lebesgue-integral-on-a-compact-interval]] and
[[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. The kernel is integrable and
$$\int_0^t(t-s)^{\beta-1}\,ds=\frac{t^\beta}{\beta}$$
by [[lem-fractional-integral-kernel-power-integral]]. Tonelli's theorem
[[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] therefore gives
$$\int_0^T\int_0^t(t-s)^{\beta-1}|g(s)|\,ds\,dt =\int_0^T|g(s)|\int_s^T(t-s)^{\beta-1}dt\,ds \le \frac{T^\beta}{\beta}\|g\|_{L^1(0,T)}<\infty,$$

open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ whose union contains $[a,b]$ has a finite subfamily
whose union already contains $[a,b]$.

subcover, one halves the interval, keeps a half that still admits none, and
iterates; the halves shrink to a point, which the cover does reach, and a single
member of the cover then swallows a whole late-stage half. **The halving rule is
canonical**, taking the left half whenever the left half works, so the recursion
uses [[thm-recursion]] and no choice principle.

[[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]].

- An **open cover** of $(X,d)$ is a family $\mathcal{U}$ of open subsets of $X$
  with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$, where
  $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily
  $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$ that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \emptyset$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,d)$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite subcover: for
  every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \emptyset$ and the empty subfamily
  covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$

  subspace $(A, d_A)$ is a compact metric space, $d_A$ being the restriction of
  $d$ to $A \times A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A,d_A)$ and its own open sets, not
about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do agree,
but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]], and no item of this library may use the
ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading as the
definition is what makes "compact" a property of the metric space $(A,d_A)$
alone, so that a set compact in one ambient space is compact in every other one
containing it isometrically.

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. The
one-point space is compact too, and so is every space listed as
$\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$: given a cover, each $x_i$ lies in some member, and
finitely many members chosen in this way already cover.

the listing form, matching the finite lists of
[[def-finite-intersection-property]]. It agrees with the definition of
finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number ([[def-countable]]), and
both directions of the agreement are available and are used below:

  $F \approx m$ for some $m \ge 1$, and a bijection $m \to F$ is exactly a
  listing $F = \{a_0, \dots, a_{m-1}\}$.
- Conversely a set listed as $A = \{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$, that is the image of a
  function $a$ with domain $\sigma(n)$, is finite in the sense of
  [[def-countable]]: the map sending $x \in A$ to the least $i \le n$ with
  $a_i = x$ is an injection of $A$ into $\sigma(n)$, so $A$ is equinumerous with
  a subset of $\mathbb{N}$ bounded above, and such a subset is finite
  ([[lem-subset-of-countable]]).

least index instead.

([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $f$ is **bounded on $K$**: there is a real
$M \ge 0$ with

$$|f(x)| \le M \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, $f[K]$ is a bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-bounded-set]]).

**The hypothesis is compactness of $K$, not of $A$**, and it cannot be relaxed
to boundedness of $K$ or to closedness of $K$ alone: the identity is unbounded
on the closed set $[0,\infty)$, and $x \mapsto 1/x$ is unbounded on the bounded
set $(0,1)$. The general statement of that is
[[thm-compactness-is-necessary-for-evt-and-uniform-continuity]], later on this
page.

**absolutely continuous** on $[a,b]$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$\delta>0$ such that every finite family of subintervals
$[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$, indexed by $j<m$, whose open interiors are pairwise
disjoint and which satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}(v_j-u_j)<\delta$$

also satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}|f(v_j)-f(u_j)|<\varepsilon.$$

Finite sums and the empty sum are those of [[def-finite-sum]] and
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. For $m=0$ both sums are $0$, so the condition is
automatic. On $[a,a]$ every permitted interval is a singleton and every endpoint
increment is $0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), so every function on that singleton is
absolutely continuous. Absolute continuity implies ordinary continuity
([[def-continuity-real]]); that implication is proved next rather than built into
the definition.

differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.
For every $s>0$, $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$, and $\Gamma(1)=1$.

For $s>0$, define $\Gamma(s)=\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$.

The integral is improper at both $0$ and $+\infty$. Its convergence for every $s>0$, and its failure for $s\le0$, are proved in [[thm-real-gamma-euler-integral-convergence]], which justifies the definition on exactly the displayed domain. The integrand is positive, so $\Gamma(s)>0$ throughout $(0,\infty)$.

For $\beta>0$ and $t>0$,
$$\int_0^t(t-s)^{\beta-1}\,ds=\frac{t^\beta}{\beta}.$$
When $0<\beta<1$ the integral is improper at $s=t$; for $\beta\ge1$ it
is an ordinary integral. It converges in both cases because
$B(\beta,1)$ is defined for positive arguments.

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

$$b_{n,k}:=\frac{(t_n-t_{k-1})^{1-\alpha}-(t_n-t_k)^{1-\alpha}}{\Gamma(2-\alpha)h_k}.$$

$$\delta_h^\alpha U^n=\frac{h^{-\alpha}}{\Gamma(2-\alpha)}\sum_{k=1}^n a_{n-k}(U^k-U^{k-1}).$$

continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that

$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one

point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does

(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

continuous integrands.

bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.
For every $s>0$, $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$, and $\Gamma(1)=1$.

$$\int_0^t(t-s)^{\beta-1}\,ds=\frac{t^\beta}{\beta}.$$
When $0<\beta<1$ the integral is improper at $s=t$; for $\beta\ge1$ it
is an ordinary integral. It converges in both cases because
$B(\beta,1)$ is defined for positive arguments.

Input $0<\alpha<1$, a step size $h>0$, an integer $N\ge1$, $\lambda\ge0$,
an initial value $u_0$, and forcing values $F^1,\ldots,F^N$. Define
$\omega_0=1$ and, for $j\ge1$,

$$\omega_j:=\frac{j-1-\alpha}{j}\,\omega_{j-1}.$$

Put $V^0=0$. For $n=1,\ldots,N$, compute

$$V^n:=\frac{F^n-\lambda u_0-h^{-\alpha}\sum_{j=1}^n\omega_jV^{n-j}}{h^{-\alpha}+\lambda},\qquad U^n:=u_0+V^n.$$

Equivalently, the discrete Caputo derivative is

$$\bar\partial_h^\alpha V^n:=h^{-\alpha}\sum_{j=0}^n\omega_jV^{n-j},$$

and the recurrence solves $\bar\partial_h^\alpha V^n+\lambda V^n=F^n-\lambda u_0$.
Since $h^{-\alpha}+\lambda>0$,
the exact-real scalar solve is nonsingular. Invalid parameters return
`invalid-input`; a finite-precision implementation that cannot certify the
solve returns `solve-failed` without reporting a value. The direct full-history
implementation uses $N(N+1)/2$ convolution terms and stores $N+1$ values; no
FFT or truncated-memory error claim is included.

Let $0<\alpha<1$ and let $(\omega_j)$ be the weights from
[[alg-backward-euler-convolution-quadrature]]. Then $\omega_0=1$,
$\omega_j<0$ for every $j\ge1$, and for every complex $z$ with $|z|<1$,
$$\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\omega_jz^j=(1-z)^\alpha_{\operatorname{Log}}.$$
For $n\ge0$ define
$$p_n:=\sum_{j=0}^n\omega_j.$$
Then
$$p_n=\prod_{k=1}^n\left(1-\frac{\alpha}{k}\right) =\frac{\Gamma(n+1-\alpha)}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)\Gamma(n+1)}>0,$$
where the empty product for $n=0$ is $1$. For every $n\ge1$,
$$p_n\ge\frac{(n+1)^{-\alpha}}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}.$$

$$x^\alpha_{\operatorname{Log}}=x^\alpha\qquad(x>0,\ \alpha\in\mathbb R).$$
For every $s>0$, $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$, and $\Gamma(1)=1$.

For $s>0$, define $\Gamma(s)=\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$.

The integral is improper at both $0$ and $+\infty$. Its convergence for every $s>0$, and its failure for $s\le0$, are proved in [[thm-real-gamma-euler-integral-convergence]], which justifies the definition on exactly the displayed domain. The integrand is positive, so $\Gamma(s)>0$ throughout $(0,\infty)$.

For $x>0$ and $0\le s\le1$, $x^{1-s}\le\Gamma(x+1)/\Gamma(x+s)\le(x+1)^{1-s}$.

For $0<s<1$ both inequalities are strict. At $s=0$ the lower inequality is equality, and at $s=1$ both are equalities.

Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals with $a_k \ne 0$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$
and put

$$q_k \;:=\; \Big|\frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k}\Big| \;=\; \frac{|a_{k+1}|}{|a_k|} \qquad (k \in \mathbb{N}),$$

a genuine sequence on $\mathbb{N}$, whose limit superior and limit inferior exist
in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ for every such $(a_k)$ ([[lem-limsup-exists]]). Then:

1. if $\limsup_{k} q_k < 1$ then $\sum |a_k|$ converges, and hence $\sum a_k$
   converges as well ([[lem-absolute-convergence-implies-convergence]]);
2. if $\liminf_{k} q_k > 1$ then $\sum a_k$ diverges.

single vanishing term leaves the ratio at that index undefined. For a family from
a starting index $m$ the statement is the one above applied to the shifted
sequence $j \mapsto a_{j+m}$ ([[def-series]]), whose ratios are
$|a_{j+m+1}/a_{j+m}|$.

regime the test is silent, and it has to be: the companion page carries a
convergent series whose ratios have limit superior $2$, and both a convergent and
a divergent series with ratio limit exactly $1$.

Let $(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a sequence of reals and let $c\in\mathbb R$. The **real power series about the centre $c$ with coefficients $(a_n)$** is the series

$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(x-c)^n$$

at a real argument $x$, where powers are those of [[def-integer-power]] and convergence is that of [[def-series]]. Its value, when the series converges, is called its **sum at $x$**. At $x=c$ the series always converges to $a_0$: the term with $n=0$ is $a_0$ because $0^0=1$, and every later term is $0$.

$$R:=\sup_{\overline{\mathbb R}}\{r\in\mathbb R:r\ge0\text{ and }P(r)\}\in[0,+\infty],$$

where the supremum is taken in the extended real line of [[def-extended-reals]]. Thus $R$ may be a nonnegative real or $+\infty$, but never $-\infty$.

The **open interval determined by the radius** is

$$I_R:=\{x\in\mathbb R:|x-c|<R\}.$$

Let

$$f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(x-c)^n$$

have radius $R$. For every $x$ with $|x-c|<R$, the function $f$ is differentiable at $x$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$f'(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\iota(n+1)a_{n+1}(x-c)^n.$$

The differentiated series has the same radius $R$.

$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

For $a,b>0$ and $r,s\in\mathbb R$,
$$a^{r+s}=a^ra^s,\qquad (ab)^r=a^rb^r,\qquad (a/b)^r=a^r/b^r,\qquad (a^r)^s=a^{rs}.$$

$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined

isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts

writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$

arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$

derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

$$f(x)g(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_kb_{n-k}\right)(x-c)^n,$$

$$f^{(m)}(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\iota\!\left((m+j)^{\underline m}\right)a_{m+j}(x-c)^j.$$

In particular,

$$f^{(m)}(c)=\iota(m!)a_m,\qquad a_m=\frac{f^{(m)}(c)}{\iota(m!)}.$$
